read in full (177 lines) against BlockProcessor.scala. Batching, per-block tokio::spawn, ordered collection with a panicked task logged and skipped rather than killing the loop, insert errors logged and the block dropped, and only validated blocks forwarded and broadcast. One divergence from the oracle, checked and assessed as deliberate rather than reported as a defect: the Scala is inputBlocks.parEvalMapUnorderedProcBounded, so it processes each block the moment its validation finishes, while this port awaits the batch's handles in drained order and inserts serially. That is required, not incidental — dag.insert refuses a block whose justification is absent (casper/src/dag.rs:293), so the inserts must follow the drain order the receiver guarantees (parents before children), and the comment says so. The cost is throughput, not correctness: a batch completes no faster than its first-listed element, bounded by the available_parallelism cap. Not registered as a deviation because the observable outcome is the same set of validated blocks in the same order; recorded here so the next reader does not have to re-derive why an Unordered in the oracle became an ordered loop. Nothing found.

create_block selects every valid pooled deploy and turns the count into a u8 for the randomness seed, so a pool of 256 makes the seed conversion fail before any state work and the proposer can never produce a block; the pool cap of 10_000 and the per-block capacity of 255 are set in different places

read in full (281 lines) against CasperConf.scala. The load-bearing part is the shard resolution and its non-emptiness. ShardSpec::new resolves (parent-shard-id, shard-name) into the validated full id through ShardId::child, so one predicate lives in one place — the type's own — and the pre-check that used to be duplicated here is gone, which is C78's shape applied correctly. ShardMemberships carries its fields private with primary always present, so non-emptiness is structural rather than re-checked at each use and primary() is total; the hardcoded is_empty() -> false says in its own comment that it exists for clippy and is total by construction, which is honest rather than a stub. new() rejects an empty list and duplicate ids, and duplicates matter for the stated reason: two memberships with one id would share a state hash and a data directory. Six tests, covering the illegal name or parent, the hierarchy resolution, non-emptiness with primary first, order plus duplicate rejection, get for a member and a non-member, and primary_mut. Nothing found.

read in full (763 lines) against LfsBlockRequester.scala, and it is the module C64 is about, so the point of the read was to see whether the code agrees with the account rather than to re-derive it. It does, and independently: validate_received_block's own comment states the full-ancestry walk with its reason verbatim — 'dag.insert requires every justification to be present in the message map, so the requester must reconstruct the full ancestry chain down to the genesis block (a syncing node's DAG is always empty)' — which is the premise I verified first-hand at casper/src/dag.rs:293 when I declined to bound the walk. The registered deviation note at the top ('minus the Scala lowerBound acceptance cutoff') matches the §6 row. C65's fix is in place with its reasoning: save_block writes and only then marks done, both through ?, so a failed write fails the sync attempt rather than being swallowed — the row's point being that marking done anyway would remove the key from the request map and leave a permanently missing block in a state the node calls synced. The instrument is here too: the_walk_advances_on_responses_not_on_the_idle_timeout at :518, the test C64's account cites for its 3.85 ms measurement. Nothing new found.

the ledger is a bare KeyValueTypedStore keyed by hash(txn_id) with plain get and put, which is the store the non-atomic check-then-act above runs on; it also has no cap and no expiry, so a scanner walks it in full

run() reads the coordinator ledger, decides there is no record, then writes one, with no lock, no per-txn_id serialization and no compare-and-set on the durable store, so two concurrent calls for one txn_id both open the transaction and the record can describe effects that were never applied

read in full (635 lines) against MultiParentCasper.scala, checking that the two fixes this file carries are where the register says they are rather than taking the rows' word. (1) C120: validate's first act is crate::validate::block_summary, and its Ok(Err(status)) arm returns ValidationFailed(mark_failed_attributable(meta), status) — so a block whose deploy signature does not match its named deployer is refused before the replay, attributably, which is what the row claims. (2) C122: mark_failed_attributable sets slashable: true, and the flag now survives the store rather than being lost — models/proto/casper.proto has 'bool slashable = 22', and block_metadata.rs carries it in from_proto (:90) and to_proto (:133). Before C122 the conversion hard-coded false, which made validate::slashable_senders always return the empty set and slashing unreachable; that is fixed and the field doc records what was wrong three ways. The three failure paths are also all attributable — a rejected status, a replay that disagrees, and Ok(false) mapped to InvalidStateHash — while a store or runtime lookup failure is Internal and gets no block outcome, which is the distinction the ValidateError doc draws. DEPLOY_LIFESPAN is pinned by value rather than as a constant, with the reason (a consensus-visible parameter, so a silent change is a chain split). Nothing new found.

read in full (846 lines) against RuntimeReplaySyntax.scala, and it earns the tier: this is where Law 11's replay determinism is actually checked. Three things checked first, since each is a place a replay check quietly stops checking. (1) The comparisons are two-sided rather than one: processed_deploy.is_failed != result.failed() and recorded_cost != result.cost.value both refuse on disagreement in either direction, and the cost conversion is a typed try_from whose overflow is a named mismatch rather than a wrap. (2) The pre-charge arm distinguishes the two things that share system_deploy_error — a play-side pre-charge failure versus a failed user deploy — by re-running the pre-charge and comparing the recorded text, with three arms (equal, unequal, and unexpected), which is the discrimination issue #15 needed. (3) The failure paths are real: a failed user deploy reverts to its soft checkpoint before the comparison, and the per-deploy phlo budget is set to match the play path with the reason written out, so a replayed deploy cannot spuriously OOG against the shared replay pool and fail the cost check for the wrong reason. R4's fix is also visible here as the Option<i64> phlo charge: an overflow is ReplayFailure::internal_error('phlo charge overflow'), not a wrapped value. That closes the coverage half — twenty modules read, two defects found and fixed (C164, C165), and no module has ever been read and cleared before this pass.

run_2pc anchored every phase deploy at block 0 (it called the 0-hardcoded run_phase wrapper), so on any chain past DEPLOY_LIFESPAN = 50 every prepare and commit was born expired: the participant never saw it, nothing reported an error, and the transaction silently did not happen. run_phase_at had been added to fix exactly this trap -- it is named as one of the sites that anchor correctly in protocol/client.rs's resolve_valid_after_block_number doc -- but the whole-transaction driver kept calling the wrapper, and run_phase_anchors_at_zero pinned that as intended. The anchor is now a required TxnLeg field, run_2pc forwards each leg's own height, and the wrapper is deleted

the read's finding, and it is fixed: write_with_mode wrote the secret first and called set_permissions afterwards, so a pre-existing 0644 rnode.key held the key world-readable for the length of the write. C8 found that the set_permissions call was missing and added it — after the write, with a comment claiming that is what keeps the content from being briefly readable. Exactly the reverse. The order is inverted, and the open-then-narrow step is split out so the order is testable: the new test asserts the mode is already narrow before anything is written, and C8's own test cannot see it because it asserts the final mode, which both orders satisfy.

read in full (447 lines) plus the call graph, against implicits.scala. The interesting question here is depth, because getting it backwards would corrupt free-variable analysis everywhere, and the answer is that the port computes the same thing by a different mechanism. In the Scala, depth is threaded through the HasLocallyFree instances and incremented at exactly two sites, both in the MatchCase instance (implicits.scala:509 and :523, locallyFree(pat, depth + 1)); locallyFree(Var) is BitSet(index) at depth 0 and empty above it, so depth counts match-case bindings and a pattern's own binder is not free. This port does not thread depth: it applies the Scala's own from_free(levels, n) — keep levels >= n and shift down by n, normalizer.rs:643, documented as the Scala BitSet.from(n).map(x => x - n) — at the two normalizer sites that correspond (normalize_new at :701 with the bound count, and the match case at :768). Same semantics, fewer parameters. The depth argument on locally_free_of_var/of_expr is therefore only exercised at 0 today: both callers pass 0 (spatial_matcher.rs:70 asks whether an expression is locally closed, reduce.rs:73 unions into the free set), and the non-zero arm is reachable but unused, which is the Scala's arm kept rather than dropped. Expr coverage is exhaustive by construction — no wildcard arm, so a new variant is a compile error rather than a silent omission. Nothing found.

read in full (151 lines) against Validator.scala: a 65-byte identity whose field is private, so the length is carried structurally; a checked TryFrom<&[u8]> returning a typed error naming both lengths, an unchecked from_slice that asserts, and serde as lowercase hex that refuses both non-hex and a wrong length. Four tests, all two-sided. Checked the one risk rather than assuming it: from_slice is the unchecked path and would panic on a short slice, so I traced every non-test caller — there is exactly one, models/src/casper/pretty_printer.rs:124, passing a fixed [0xcd; 65] literal (the other apparent caller, validator_identity.rs:85, is inside a #[test]). So the doc's claim that callers carry the invariant structurally holds today. One thing recorded without calling it a defect, because nothing reaches it: PublicKey is a bare Vec<u8> with an unchecked new(), so from_slice(&public_key.bytes()) would be a panic rather than an error — a footgun for the next caller, not a live defect.

written and reviewed in this session while closing AUDIT C144, so the review is the authoring: the file is the node's whole stop path — the signal handler, the watch channel every listener awaits, and the bounded drain timeout. **Both directions measured, and the review found one defect in its own first draft.** With `wait_for` replaced by a plain borrow (so `stop_requested` resolves immediately) the unit test's first arm fails — "a listener must not stop before the coordinator asks it to"; and with `acquire_http_server`'s `with_graceful_shutdown` removed, `node/tests/shutdown.rs` fails at "the HTTP listener must be closed after the stop, not merely unreported". The defect: a listener that drains *because it was told to* returns `Ok(())`, and the first draft's `listener_stopped` read that as "an accept loop returned" — so `docker stop` would sometimes have reported a server error and exited 1 on a perfectly clean shutdown, decided by `select!`'s arbitrary choice among ready arms. The `stopping` flag is that fix. Not read: the transport layer's own shutdown (`comm/src/transport/grpc_transport_receiver.rs`), which is the residue C144's own row names — this file hands it nothing to await.

read in full (402 lines) against ContractCall.scala, plus the caller. The load-bearing part is native_body_ref, which derives a continuation id from (name_bytes, arity) and forces it negative with | i64::MIN so it cannot collide with a small non-negative BodyRefs constant. Checked the two things that could be wrong. (1) The derivation is a function of the name and the arity and not of a counter, and the doc says why that matters here: a counter would depend on how many handles this dispatcher has installed, and replay builds a fresh dispatcher, so the continuation would dispatch nowhere on the second run — a real replay-determinism trap avoided. (2) The id is negative by construction, and a channel can carry several arities under one name, which is exactly the oracle vault's shape (balance at 2, transfer at 5), so the arity has to be part of the id. The one risk I looked for is a non-positive arity, since install_native builds (0..arity) patterns and sets free_count from it: the single caller (system_processes.rs:433) passes integer literals 2 and 5 in a loop, so it is unreachable. install_native also registers before installing, deliberately, so a failure leaves a handler nobody can reach rather than a continuation that dispatches into an empty table. Nothing found.

read in full (447 lines) against dispatch.scala, plus its tests. The thing I looked for is the one this crate's clippy debt list would hide: await_holding_lock is in the allow-list, so a lock held across an await here would never be reported. It is not — both dispatch arms take the table's lock in an inner block, call the handler to produce a future, drop the guard at the end of that block, and await outside it. That is the correct pattern and it is deliberate rather than lucky. Three further properties, each checked rather than assumed. (1) register_handler is idempotent per id and says why that is required rather than lazy: the install path re-runs on replay and a deploy may legitimately call findOrCreate twice for one address in a block, so the second call must reach the same handler rather than swap a new closure under a continuation the space already holds; the check-then-insert is under the table's own lock, so two concurrent installs cannot both win. (2) The ParBody arm does not sort its random states, with a comment saying so and why: the order is continuation-first then matched data in receive-bind order, matching dispatch.scala:33, and data_list is already canonical — sorting here would break the determinism it looks like it protects. (3) A missing evaluator is BugFoundError rather than a silent no-op, which is the shape this register keeps asking for. Eight tests, including that an unregistered ref is refused by name and that a dropped dispatcher is reported through the Weak handle. Nothing found.

read in full (57 lines) against its oracle while closing R32's wave. The codec is 32 bytes fixed, decode refuses any other length by name before constructing a hash, and both halves are pinned by a round trip that asserts the exact bytes and a four-length refusal arm. One interface difference from the Scala and it is the safer direction: scodec's codec is stream-based, so bytes(size = length) decodes a 32-byte prefix and leaves the remainder, while this Codec::decode is whole-value and refuses a 33-byte input that scodec would have accepted; a store handing back the wrong value length is a corruption, and refusing it is what a key codec should do.

read in full (103 lines) against HistoryAction.scala: two variants, a key() accessor and a trim() that drops one byte for both, with three tests. **The one thing worth naming is already registered, and that is the finding:** trim() on an empty key panics, because KeySegment::tail indexes value[1..], and a #[should_panic] test pins it rather than a guard preventing it. That is not new here and it is not a defect this read found, it is C61's recorded residual: the tree never trims past a leaf, the panic is latent, and C61's account says in as many words that the pass leaves it there because carrying the invariant would be the ~30-site rewrite its plan calls option 7. Recorded as read-and-already-registered rather than re-reported, because a reader of this row should be able to tell a new defect from a known one.

read in full (450 lines) against HistoryRepository.scala and HistoryRepositoryImpl.scala, completing the history cluster. The constants are the thing that would silently corrupt every state hash, so they were checked first and against the definition rather than inferred: PREFIX_DATUM 0x00, PREFIX_KONT 0x01, PREFIX_JOINS 0x02, exactly as HistoryRepository.scala:53-55 has them. calculate_storage_action is arm-for-arm the Scala's calculateStorageActions — encode the leaf, encode the leaf-with-its-tag, hash it, and return (hash, leaf) beside InsertAction(KeySegment(PREFIX +: hash.bytes), leaf_hash). The checkpoint ordering is the other property that matters and it is right: cold leaves are written before the trie actions that reference them, and the write is put-if-absent (contains, filter, put) — a repeated leaf is the same bytes under the same hash, so the check-then-act is idempotent rather than a race with a consequence. A failed cold write propagates before the trie is touched, so a checkpoint cannot leave a trie pointing at leaves that are not there. Three tests; the two interesting ones are that two repositories over the same stores agree on the root, and that resetting to an unknown root is an error. Nothing found.

read in full (93 lines) against RootRepository.scala, and it is line-for-line faithful: commit delegates to recordRoot, current_root records and returns the empty root on a first read (the Scala's None arm), and validate_and_set_current_root turns the store's refusal into an error. The one difference is the error's shape, not its meaning: the Scala raises RuntimeException("unknown root") and the port returns Err("unknown root"), which is this tree's error convention on every trait it converted (Result<_, String>). Both behaviours are pinned two-sidedly: an empty store yields and records the empty root AND the validated setter then accepts it, and a refused root leaves the current root where it was rather than moving to a root that does not exist.

the read's finding, and it is fixed: current_root handed the store's value straight to Blake2b256Hash::from_byte_array, which asserts a 32-byte length, so a truncated current-root panicked the node on the path every state read goes through. One file over, codecs.rs performs the identical conversion and does guard it — the discipline existed and was not applied where the same bytes are read. Guarded now, falsified both ways.

read in full (748 lines) against ReplayRSpace.scala, Law 11's replay determinism. The checker is the thing to look at and it is in the state C152 recorded: check_replay_data reads the replay-data map and errors with Unused COMM event and the count when it is not empty, so a recorded COMM the replay never produced is a refusal rather than a pass — and it is not the neutered form C152's row describes ('if data.is_empty()' changed to 'if true'), which would have made it answer Ok unconditionally. Both error directions C152 named are present and at the lines it named: a_rigged_replay_matches_its_recorded_trace at :703 and a_rig_whose_comm_never_happens_is_reported at :731. The ReplayData bookkeeping backs it: comms_for_consume/comms_for_produce hand out the recorded COMMs, remove_*_binding drops each one as it is used and prunes the emptied key, so 'every recorded COMM was used' is exactly is_empty() and the count in the error is the number left over. This is the second read whose finding was already registered and already fixed — like history_action's C61 and codecs' guard, the value of the read is confirming the fix is where the register says it is rather than taking the row's word. Nothing new found.

read in full (494 lines) against the Laws 20-22 model, and the soundness claim is the thing to check: the module's own doc says phase-one reads are advisory and phase two re-validates atomically, because the candidate may have been consumed by a cross-channel op in the gap. It does. scheduled_produce_commit computes its lock set from the *current* join groups (the phase_two thunk reads get_joins at acquisition time rather than reusing phase one's set) and then runs scheduled_produce_commit_body, which re-reads the joins and re-extracts under that lock, falling back to storing the datum when nothing matches. So a join set that changed in the gap is locked as it is now and decided on as it is now, not as phase one saw it — which is what makes deliberate hold-and-wait across trigger plus join channels safe rather than a race. The arm that would catch a regression is pinned by its own test: a_commit_whose_candidate_vanished_stores_instead_of_delivering. The consume genuinely needs no split, as the doc says, because its full static source set is claimed up front. Five tests. Nothing found.

the only installed logger prints level, class and message with no wall-clock time, debug and trace are empty bodies and is_trace_enabled is hardcoded false, so incident forensics are ordering-only and cross-node timelines cannot be reconstructed from the logs

read in full (76 lines): a fixed window with a Mutex-guarded window_start and an AtomicU64 count. Three things checked, since this is the DoS bound several unauthenticated surfaces rest on. (1) The bound holds, and the atomic read-modify-write is what makes it hold: allow() returns count.fetch_add(1) < max_per_sec, so at most max_per_sec callers can ever observe a value below the cap within a window — a plain load-then-store would admit an unbounded number under contention. (2) The counts reset per window and a refused request still increments, which cannot admit more than the cap and cannot overflow a u64 in a one-second window. (3) The one real limitation is already registered and is not this module's: the limiter is per-surface and not per-client, so one caller can spend the whole budget for everyone — that is R17's finding, recorded against the faucet and the ingress class, and it is a property of where the limiters are installed rather than of this type. Window rollover can lose an increment when a reset races another thread's fetch_add; the effect is to admit a couple more across a boundary, which is the shape of a fixed window and not a defect. Three tests, including that zero closes the surface rather than making it unlimited. Nothing found.
